object_description: staggered clinic ensemble of parallel and transverse volumes
design_condition: The building follows the existing edge and slope, creating a three-sided open-space ensemble with a small park on the mountain side, while excavations and an undefined opening weaken its relationship to the neighbourhood and park.

positive.statement: The center-and-periphery concept offers a promising basis for an ensemble with the existing buildings.
Staggered heights and facade setbacks adapt the building to the district and achieve a compatible scale.
The small mountain-side park can serve as open space for both the district and the clinic.
The entrance situation on Hofstrasse is clear and uncluttered.
The entrance hall creates a cheerful atmosphere and an attractive interplay between indoor and outdoor spaces.
The clinic-room arrangement enables the desired separation between staff and patients.
The polyclinic can be converted to a new use with only a few structural interventions.
The connection to the new building is a precise and coherent intervention inherent in the existing typology and concept.
The urban-planning concept is robust with regard to future preservation, replacement, or release of the sisters' house.
The result is valuable for the historical inventory and its perception.
The independent facade forms an ensemble with the character buildings while creating a familiar expression.
The hybrid wood-concrete construction conceptually takes sustainability requirements into account.
Resource-saving and lean materialization compensate to a large extent for the effort required under the terrain.

negative.statement: The green space along Pestalozzistrasse has little quality and resembles distance green.
The opening toward the neighbourhood lacks a clear spatial definition.
The proposed excavation along the north-east facade can hardly be approved under building regulations in its current form.
The three atriums obscure the relationship between the new building and the park.
The paths are functional, but a self-confident park character is missing.
The main entrance appears too large and too stony.
The adjacent seating area does not appear self-evident, and preserving the existing trees will hardly be possible.
The sudden transitions from the large entrance hall to corridors and stairwells were critically assessed.
Crossing access routes and internal clinic waiting rooms are spatially and operationally problematic.
The underground teaching area without daylight did not convince the jury.
There is no direct connection between teaching and research without passing through the clinics.
The wooden roller shutters do not optimally meet the requirements for shading and daylight control.
The contribution is one of the more complex proposals in terms of economic efficiency.
The project requires relatively large floor area and underbuilds a significant part of the plot.
The insulation, airtightness, facade construction, and summer thermal protection require further development to achieve the required standard.
Spatially dividing excavations and weak relationships between the garden and new building contradict the idea of strengthening the hospital garden as a center.
